hypotheses.scope: Provisional board judgments recorded after fixed game export and before fresh engine/classifier output. Not final gold or a claim that quiet-looking positions contain no tactic.

cases.judgment: Closed Sicilian development; d3/Nge2/castling is ordinary coordination, not a concrete forced tactical motif.
Black can challenge White's flank expansion with central d5. A pawn break is not automatically a tactical clearance or sacrifice; concrete all-reply gain would need proof.
White has space and a potential kingside attack. Bishop improvement or defensive coordination alone should not become a pin/fork; a useful immediate forcing resource is unresolved.

After Rf1 rather than the known stronger Bf1, Black can countercheck with Qd4+ before collecting e5. Check whether this is a saving/defensive attack or only a material concession; do not assume the prior mating threat still forces a win.
Ordinary French Advance/Tarrasch-style development. White supports the centre and develops; no discrete root material combination expected.

Black has sacrificed the a-pawn to damage White's queenside. Bishop access to a3 and knight development need concrete net accounting; recovering a pawn should not be counted as independent profit without full history.

Nc4 attacks the queen on c2 and a knight/pin relationship involves Bb5 and Na5. A queen retreat or trade may simply answer one threat. Determine actual best purpose before calling multiple geometrical relationships tactics.
Black can target loose b5 while White has checking activity. Queen repositioning toward a pawn is not itself a skewer/fork; verify whether a immediate concrete material collection is available.
Qxe6+ recovers the pawn on e6 immediately after fxe6. Whole game history matters: it is not automatically a free pawn. Possible subsequent mating/queen activity is unresolved.
White needs ordinary development in a restrained opening. Nf3/Bb5 pressure must not become a tactical pin without a forcing payoff.
The f6 knight is attacked by g5. Its retreat may open Qxg5 or a king attack, but vacating a queen diagonal alone is not a proved root clearance. Tactical preparation remains unresolved.
exd4 recaptures the bishop that just took White's bishop. This equal exchange is not a newly hung bishop; a distinct stronger king-safety resource must remain separate.
Bxd3/Qxd3 recovers the advanced pawn after e4xd3 in an opening gambit. Include all earlier pawn exchanges; development and recovery are not an independent pawn win.
Bxf6 recaptures the knight that just took Black's knight and checked the king. Equal minor-piece exchange, not a freshly hung knight or independent defender-removal win.
f4 gains a tempo on Ne5, which can retreat to f7. A single pawn attack is not a fork/trap; possible independent captures elsewhere need their own proof.

Rxc2 appears to collect an undefended pawn but the exposed king and major-piece coordination make compensation relevant. Do not turn later mutual checks into a root attraction or assume a material loss from one PV.

White's f1 bishop blocks the rooks' route to Kg1. Qf3 can allow a queen/bishop for two rooks liquidation: that is not a sequence of independent free-piece gains. The best move and whether a saving tactical mechanism is necessary remain unresolved.

Black's king must manage White's queenside passers. A quiet king move or later promotion in the game does not establish a current root tactic/zugzwang. Do not infer exact endgame outcome from a short line.
